title: Object, Map & Set
lede: A two-tier object model. Statically-typed objects are fixed-shape heap structs — compile-time field offsets, real per-heap-identity Object.freeze, compile-time Object.hasOwn. Dynamic objects (any-typed values, untyped JSON, js-mode literals) are real property bags with prototype chains (Object.create, __proto__), property descriptors (defineProperty, accessors, enumerability, descriptor-backed freeze/seal), and runtime add/delete. Map and Set carry the full core API; where JS says Iterable, this compiler narrows to a concrete array, and a missing Map key reads back as the null stand-in.

entries.name: Object literals { a: 1 }
entries.signature: let point: { x: number; y: number } = { x: 10, y: 20 }
entries.description: Object literals build fixed-shape heap structs. The type may be annotated or inferred from the initializer; objects pass by reference (heap pointer), so a mutation through a function parameter is visible to the caller.
entries.snippet:
let point: { x: number; y: number } = { x: 10, y: 20 }
console.log(point.x)   // 10

entries.name: Field access obj.field
entries.description: Reads and writes to a struct field by name, including compound assignment. Field access is a compile-time resolved struct offset.
entries.snippet:
point.x = 30
point.y += 5
console.log(point.y)   // 25

entries.name: Object destructuring
entries.description: Binds fields of an object to local variables by name in a single declaration.

entries.name: Object.keys(obj)
entries.description: Returns a string[] of the object's field names in declaration order. The result can be iterated directly without an intermediate variable.

entries.name: Object.values(obj)
entries.description: Returns a string[] of each field value converted to a string, in declaration order.

entries.name: Object.entries(obj)
entries.description: Returns a real [string, string][] tuple array; destructure with for (const [k, v] of Object.entries(obj)).
differences: Values are stringified — a heterogeneous object's value type is a union not yet representable

entries.name: Object.groupBy(arr, fn)
entries.description: Groups an array's elements by the string key each returns from fn, producing a dynamic object mapping each key to the array of its members. Access groups by key and enumerate them via Object.keys.

entries.name: Object.assign(target, ...src)
entries.description: Copies each source's fields into target in argument order — a later source overwrites an earlier one on a shared field. Mutates and returns target (same heap object, no copy).
entries.snippet:
const applied = Object.assign(defaults, userPrefs)
console.log(defaults.theme)     // dark (same object)
differences: Every field a source contributes must already exist on `target`'s struct type — a source field `target`'s type doesn't have is a clean compile error (fixed-shape heap structs), not grafted on as in real JS

entries.name: Object.defineProperty / getOwnPropertyDescriptor / accessors
entries.description: Real property descriptors on dynamic (any-typed, or js-mode untyped-literal) objects: defineProperty with the spec's create defaults and non-configurable redefinition rules, getOwnPropertyDescriptor in both data and accessor forms, getOwnPropertyNames including non-enumerables, and object-literal get/set accessors invoked with the original receiver — inherited getters through the prototype chain included. Object.keys, for...in, and JSON.stringify honor enumerability (stringify and spread invoke getters), and rejected writes or deletes throw the module-strict JS TypeErrors. Object.freeze/seal/preventExtensions enforce through the same attributes, with truthful isFrozen/isSealed/isExtensible. Statically-typed structs have no descriptor table; Object.defineProperties is a follow-on.

entries.name: new Proxy(target, handler)
entries.description: Proxies over dynamic objects with the get, set, has and deleteProperty traps dispatched inside the object runtime itself — property reads, writes, the in operator and delete on a proxy all consult the handler, and forward straight to the target when a trap is absent. JSON.stringify of a proxy serializes the target. Other traps (ownKeys, apply, construct, getOwnPropertyDescriptor) are not consulted, and statically-typed structs can't be proxied.

entries.name: Reflect
entries.description: The Reflect surface mapped 1:1 onto the dynamic-object runtime: get, set, has, deleteProperty, ownKeys, getPrototypeOf, setPrototypeOf, isExtensible, preventExtensions and defineProperty. The boolean-returning forms (set, deleteProperty, setPrototypeOf) return the success flag instead of throwing, per spec. Reflect.apply and Reflect.construct are missing, and targets must be dynamic objects.

entries.name: Object.create() / getPrototypeOf / setPrototypeOf / __proto__
entries.description: Real prototype chains on dynamic (any-typed) objects: Object.create(proto or null), get/setPrototypeOf, the __proto__ accessor (non-object assignments silently ignored, as in JS), and the { __proto__: base } literal form. Property reads and the in operator walk the chain — an own property shadows an inherited one, and delete re-exposes the prototype's value — while writes, Object.keys, for...in, and JSON.stringify stay own-only, matching JS. A prototype cycle throws the Node-matching TypeError. Statically-typed structs have no prototype link (the two-tier model), and Object.create's property-descriptors second argument is not yet supported.

entries.name: Object.freeze(obj)
entries.description: Real runtime enforcement, not a no-op: tracks obj's heap pointer in a global frozen-object set, checked at every field-write site, so a blocked write throws a catchable Error even through a different alias or function parameter. Adding/deleting fields is already structurally impossible, so value-write is the only thing freeze needs to enforce.

entries.name: Object.seal(obj)
entries.description: A genuine no-op, not a scope-narrowed approximation: seal's guarantee ("no new/deleted fields") is already structurally impossible for this compiler's fixed-shape objects, so there's nothing further to enforce — existing fields stay freely writable.
entries.snippet:
Object.seal(sealed)
sealed.port = 2
console.log(sealed.port)  // 2 (seal never blocked the value write)

entries.name: Object.hasOwn() / .hasOwnProperty()
entries.description: Field-presence check. Object shapes are fully structural/static, so this is a compile-time FieldIndex lookup, not a runtime scan. The `in` operator applies the same check as an operator form.

returns.desc: Whether the field exists on the object.

entries.snippet:
console.log(Object.hasOwn(base, 'x'))     // 1
console.log(base.hasOwnProperty('q'))     // 0
console.log('x' in base)                  // 1
differences: The key must be a string literal — a runtime-computed key is a clean compile error (no runtime field-name table to check it against)

entries.name: Object.fromEntries()
entries.description: Returns a dynamic object (a Map<string,V>-backed value); read via obj.field / obj[key]. Seeds via the same [K,V][] walker new Map(entries) uses.
differences: Keys must be strings (a `[string, V][]` array) — real JS stringifies any key and accepts symbol keys

entries.name: Object spread { ...obj, key: val }
entries.description: Copies a source object's fields, then applies later properties in source order — a property mentioned again simply overwrites the earlier value. Spread is a shallow copy: nested object fields are shared, not cloned. A spread may also add new fields not present on the source.

entries.name: Computed property keys { [expr]: value }
entries.description: A dynamic object — storage-wise a real Map<string,V> reusing new Map<K,V>()'s runtime, with .field / [expr] sugar layered on top. A well-known-symbol key (Symbol.asyncIterator / Symbol.iterator) is the exception: it desugars to a reserved static key so the literal stays a static struct driving for...of / for await...of.
entries.snippet:
const k = 'b'
const obj = { a: 1, [k]: 2 }
console.log(obj[k])     // 2
obj['c'] = 99
console.log(obj.c)      // 99
differences: `V` is inferred from the first property only
`...spread` combined with a computed key isn't supported yet
The declared-type form (`{ [key: string]: T }`) isn't supported yet

entries.name: Shorthand property { x }
entries.description: `{ x }` is sugar for `{ x: x }`, referencing the in-scope variable of the same name. Shorthand and explicit properties can be mixed freely.
entries.snippet:
let sx: number = 5
let sy: number = 6
let shorthandPoint = { sx, sy }
console.log(shorthandPoint.sx)   // 5

entries.name: Method shorthand { foo() {...} }
entries.description: Desugars to { foo: function() {...} } — a plain anonymous function value, reusing the same closure machinery. A string-literal key can carry a method body too.
differences: No `this` binding at all — `this` inside a method-shorthand body is a clean compile-time rejection (an object literal has no nominal type to give `this` a shape, and no dynamic call-site binding machinery exists), not silently wrong
No `async`/generator method shorthand either, matching this compiler's class methods

entries.name: Map.set/get/has/delete/keys/values
entries.signature: new Map<K, V>(); m.set(k, v); m.get(k); m.has(k); m.delete(k); m.keys()
entries.description: .get() on a scalar-valued map returns V | null — a missing key is distinguishable from a stored 0/false via the presence-flagged nullable-scalar representation.
differences: A missing key reads as `null` (the compiler's `undefined` stand-in), not a distinct `undefined`; a reference-typed `V` (string/object) returns the `"null"` stand-in on a miss

entries.name: Map.size
entries.description: The number of entries currently in the map.

entries.name: Map.entries()
entries.description: Returns a real [K, V][] tuple array; iterate with for (const [k, v] of m.entries()).

entries.name: Map.forEach()
entries.description: Calls fn(value, key, map), matching real JS's full callback signature; the 3rd argument is the map being iterated. A callback declaring fewer parameters receives only the leading ones.

entries.name: Map.clear()
entries.description: Resets size to 0 in place — doesn't free/reallocate the backing arrays ("leak by design" memory model); immediately reusable afterward.

entries.name: new Map(entries)
entries.description: K/V are inferred from the entries when no <K, V> is given; duplicate keys resolve last-wins; the entries source may be a bare literal or an already-declared [K, V][] variable.
entries.snippet:
const prices = new Map([["pen", 2], ["notebook", 5], ["eraser", 1]]);
console.log(prices.get("notebook")); // 5
differences: Accepts only a `[K, V][]` array of 2-tuples, narrowed from the spec's `Iterable<[K, V]>` — the only iterable/pair concept a general expression has here

entries.name: new Set(iterable)
entries.description: Pre-populates a set from an array, collapsing duplicates. K/V type inferred from the elements, or given explicitly with <T>.
entries.snippet:
const fromLiteral = new Set([1, 2, 3, 2, 1]);
console.log(fromLiteral.size); // 3
differences: Accepts only an array expression, narrowed from the spec's `Iterable<T>` — the only iterable concept a general expression has here

entries.name: Set.add/has/delete/values
entries.signature: new Set<T>(); s.add(v); s.has(v); s.delete(v); s.values()
entries.description: Adds, tests membership, removes, and enumerates elements. Adding a value already present is a no-op.

entries.name: Set.size
entries.description: The number of distinct elements currently in the set.
entries.snippet:
console.log(ids.size);    // 2
console.log(ids.has(20)); // 1

entries.name: Set.forEach()
entries.description: Calls fn(value, value, set) — real JS's Set.prototype.forEach passes the value twice (Map/Set callback-shape parity) then the set itself; each argument is supplied per the callback's declared arity.

entries.name: Set.clear()
entries.description: Removes every element, size drops to 0, set stays usable. Same in-place reset as Map.clear().

entries.name: WeakMap / WeakSet / WeakRef
entries.signature: new WeakMap(); new WeakSet(); new WeakRef(obj)
entries.description: Object-identity-keyed weak collections and references. Under -mm=gc these are genuinely weak via Boehm disappearing links (a collected referent's .deref() / WeakMap.has observably drops); gc() forces a full collection under gc, a no-op under manual.
differences: Object-identity keys only (a primitive key is a clean compile error); non-iterable (no `size`/iteration — matches spec)
Under `-mm=manual` (default) a weak reference is strong: nothing is ever collected, so `.deref()` never nulls and keys persist ("leak by design"). Real weak semantics require `-mm=gc`
A `new WeakMap()` initial-entries argument is out of V1 scope
